title: Rejoining UNIDO: Reform, Results, and Why It Matters
label: 15 Sep 2026 · UNIDO evidence
summary: The International Agreements Committee questioned UNIDO officials about whether the UK should rejoin the organisation after leaving in 2012. Witnesses described major reforms—tripled funding, doubled project delivery, and a new focus on private-sector partnerships—and argued that membership would give the UK a seat at the table to hold UNIDO accountable and shape its future. Committee members pressed hard on whether UNIDO can scale up projects, deliver value for money, and make a real difference on the ground, especially on energy access and food security.

chapters.title: What's changed since the UK left?
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO says it has undergone painful but successful reforms that tripled funding and doubled delivery, making it a more efficient and attractive partner.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We're pleased to have you here to talk about UNIDO and the UK rejoining. Lord German will start.

turns.speaker: Lord German
turns.text: This is a what-has-changed question. What have you done since the UK withdrew that solves the problems the UK had back then?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: It's an honour to be here. I joined around the time of the UK withdrawal, so I have some history. The UK's decision was very rationally explained—there was a pillar assessment with clear conclusions about alignment with UK priorities and value for money. The mandate was never really in doubt; it was about the efficiency of the organisation.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Since then, especially under the current Director-General, we've done two major restructurings. We cut a whole layer of hierarchy—without letting anyone go, just not replacing retirees. We've strengthened financial management, procurement, HR and talent management. We've become a more efficient implementer.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: In four years we've tripled our funds mobilisation and doubled our technical delivery on the ground. This year we'll reach £400 million in delivery. The UK has become our second largest donor, which is impressive and shows it sees the win-win.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The UK gave us a test-case project of £80 million, later increased to about £140 million, because it was done well. We've also opened the organisation up to private business—something unique in the UN space. We're the partner that brings technology, know-how and companies to partner countries.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Several member states, even very critical Governments, are pulling funds from other organisations and giving them to us. They say it's because we can justify a clear business interest—we get them into interesting markets in Africa, Latin America and Asia. So we're growing and on a good financial footing, but there's much more to do.

chapters.title: Energy access and private investment
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses acknowledge the huge gaps in energy investment but argue UNIDO is shifting from just providing access to using energy as a driver for industrial development.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: I visit developing nations all the time, and I struggle to see why so little investment goes into energy. I just came back from the DRC, where large swathes have no electricity. I'm puzzled about where your resources are targeted and how you measure outcomes with the private sector.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Thank you for that question. It's true—only a handful of countries benefit from energy investments. Least developed countries and small island states still need much more. We host forums to discuss financial flows and we work at the national level on industrial transformation investment plans.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Energy isn't just about lighting; it's about comfort and industrial development. UNIDO uniquely brings the idea that energy is the backbone but industry is the engine for development. We're working with west Africa, for example, on economic corridors for mineral beneficiation—moving beyond just energy access to energy as a transformational opportunity.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: The frustration is that while you may do the macro-industrial picture, most of those countries depend on very small industries developing, and that's not happening because they can't get energy at all. Sometimes we need to start where growth can actually happen with local people on the ground.

chapters.title: UN reform and UNIDO's role
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO claims it's ahead of the UN80 reform curve and is now focused on clarifying its unique role and outsourcing back-office functions where others are better.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: You've helpfully set out your reforms. But all UN institutions are under severe pressure on contributions. What contribution is UNIDO making to the Secretary-General's efforts to reduce civil servants and programmes?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: UN80 is very important. We had to do a lot of that work already—that's how we pre-empted some shocks. Our role is to be very specific about who is good at what. There's often a blurred area between us and UNDP or FAO. We've been working at New York level to flesh out the different mandates and value additions.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: We're looking honestly at what internal structures we're duplicating. Why can't we use procurement services from agencies that are better, like UNOPS or WFP? We need to see whether we need our own HR, contracts and payroll functions. We have the engineers and economists, but we might not be the best HR specialists.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: A practical example: we've partnered with UNOOSA, the space agency. We recognised industrial development relies on connectivity and geospatial data. We're now developing joint projects like Space4Industry, using AI and digital twins for early warning systems to protect industrial zones against climate risks. That's UN80 reform in action.

chapters.title: Concrete results from UK funding
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO gives examples of UK-funded work, including global carbon accounting standards for steel and cement, and on-the-ground projects like hydrogen in Namibia and biogas in Kenya.

turns.speaker: Lord Stevenson of Balmacara
turns.text: You mentioned you've gained money from the UK. Could you give us two or three concrete examples of what's happened on the ground with UK money?

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: First, on the global stage, we're working on carbon accounting standards for steel and cement—essential for global trade. Second, we're linking UK innovation ecosystems with Brazil on industrial decarbonisation, bringing universities and SMEs to support Brazil's roadmap.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Third, through the A2D Facility, we're supporting groundbreaking projects in developing countries—like Namibia's first hydrogen production programme and biogasification in the Kenyan tea industry. These bring UK technology and know-how to developing countries for productive use.

chapters.title: Food security and scaling up
chapters.takeaway: A rice project in Ghana shows how technology can cut post-harvest losses, but committee members push for more evidence of scaling up and warn against ignoring local expertise like agronomists.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: Over decades the UK taxpayer has invested in food security and linking farmers to markets. Can you give practical examples of how UNIDO's work, perhaps with FAO, has contributed? If not, please write to us. We need to demonstrate the difference UK money makes to ordinary people.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: A practical example from Ghana. About 50% of rice is imported, and 20% of local production was lost post-harvest. We developed a tool where farmers can scan the rice and track where problems occur. In six months we've reduced losses from 20% to 13% and hope to replicate it across west Africa.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: This project was funded by Japan, not the UK, but it shows how harnessing local innovation, working with farmers and bringing in the private sector can use new technology to solve food security challenges.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Alongside technology, agronomists are the greatest asset any local community can have. They understand the soil better than anybody. While your technology may help, you could eradicate the problem 100% by making sure agronomists are in the mix.

chapters.title: Why rejoin? The case for membership
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO argues that as the UK is already a major contributor, membership would give it a seat at the governing table to shape policy, ensure accountability, and secure long-term influence.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are you doing that we can't do? We already have a large development office. Why do we need to rejoin UNIDO? That's the question we'll be asked.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: It's a question all member states ask. First, we have a large network of partners. Japan is giving us £200 million for Ukraine's recovery—they see interesting growth markets and use our network. Italy is third after the UK and focuses on coffee value chains like Illy and Lavazza. They want our certification for sustainability.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: For the UK, we can help companies get a foot in the door in markets where bilateral channels aren't enough. But the political element is key: if you're already one of the biggest contributors, you want a say in the governing bodies. You're not formally a stakeholder now.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Being a member gives you due diligence and oversight over how money is spent. It's better to be part of the policy-making organs than just a contributor with no control. The membership fee is small compared to your voluntary contributions, so it's almost a no-brainer to become a member and hold us accountable.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: I can't see any good reason for joining except becoming part of a talking shop. The reality is that money we're spending isn't making a difference. Running water isn't available in many parts of the world. Why isn't it better value to spearhead projects through our own agencies?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: This is personal for me. I spent years in the field—in Chad we built solar mini-grids, in Madagascar small hydropower. Seeing energy access for irrigation, clinics and food processing is tangible. We used to do pilot projects; now the average project is £200 million because the private sector is involved. The scale is completely different.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: In Ukraine, we have a large-scale green recovery programme funded by Japan. FCDO and Innovate Ukraine reached out to us because we have access on the ground that they didn't have. It's not a transaction—it's a partnership that clearly works and benefits both parties.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: Is that not evidence that we'd be better to continue funding projects where we have mutual interest, rather than join?

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: No, because there's a next step. When a project finishes, how do we leverage further investment? That's why we established the finance coalition at London Climate Action Week—to amplify impact through private financing.

chapters.title: Scalability and long-term commitment
chapters.takeaway: The committee presses on scale and whether reforms will outlast the current Director-General; UNIDO points to institutional changes and leadership development, but acknowledges more work is needed.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: A failure in development has been the inability to scale up projects. What we need is practical examples of how you've helped scaling up. Without that, we'll miss the Sustainable Development Goals.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury
turns.text: Can you convince my sceptical colleagues what you mean by it being better to be inside, and that we're not just talking about getting caught up in bureaucracy?

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: It seems you're offering scalability we can't get as a single player. But what's to say reforms won't go back when the Director-General retires? This is a long-term commitment.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: It's about being part of this growth story. We want the UK involved in our next steps—better results-based management, communications, IT infrastructure. Other member states won't allow subcontracts or procurement if you're not a member. Beyond technical co-operation, we have a normative function and research capacity where the UK is a prime example.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The Director-General was very UN-sceptical and private-sector oriented. What we've done in a few years is promising. Other UN agencies now approach us to learn. Being part of this ensures the sustainability of this trend and keeps UK know-how with us. We're better off with you than alone.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: I've been at UNIDO longer than these two and have seen the change. The Director-General is putting in a foundation beyond his own term. We're working through implementation patterns, embedding with the private sector, and looking at new financial instruments like a transformation fund. Those are key beyond back-office reforms.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: On energy, things aren't scaling because rural demand is low. Industries provide the anchor load to make the business case. We're helping countries prepare for bigger financial flows and private sector capital. We also need concessional financing. That's the alignment we're trying to bring.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: You build institutions, but there are people behind them. The Director-General has been keen on leadership training to carry the legacy. There's a lot of enthusiasm to keep flying the flag for this organisation, which is at the centre of international collaboration on industry, trade and energy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you very much. That's been hugely helpful. We appreciate your journey from Vienna and are extremely grateful. Have a safe journey back home.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury
turns.text: Please keep supporting Lavazza.
